There have been a number of conditionality principles proposed in statistics, beginning with Fisher (always condition on an ancillary statistic when one exists). The most well-known '''conditionality principle''' is the principle of [[statistical inference]] that [[Allan Birnbaum]] formally defined and studied in an article in the ''[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]'', {{harvp|Birnbaum|1962}}. 

Informally, his conditionality principle can be taken as the claim that
: ''Experiments which were not actually performed are not relevant to any statistical analysis''
and the implicit admonition that unrealized experiments should be ignored: Not included as part of any calculation or discussion of results.

Together with the [[sufficiency principle]], Birnbaum's version of the principle implies the famous [[likelihood principle]]. However, by 1970 Birnbaum had rejected both his own conditionality principle and the likelihood principle because they were both incompatible with what he called the “confidence concept of statistical evidence”.<ref name=Birnbaum1970>

==Formulation==
The conditionality principle makes an assertion about a composite experiment, <math>\ E\ ,</math> that can be described as a suite or assemblage of several constituent experiments <math>\ E_h\ ;</math> the index <math>\ h\ </math> is some ''[[ancillary statistic]]'', i.e. a statistic whose [[probability distribution]] does not depend on any unknown [[Statistical parameter|parameter]] values. This means that obtaining an observation of some specific outcome <math>\ x\ </math> of the whole experiment <math>\ E\ </math> requires first observing a value for <math>\ h\ ,</math> and then taking an observation <math>\ x_h\ </math> from the indicated component experiment <math>\ E_h ~.</math>

The conditionality principle can be formally stated thus:
:'''Birnbaum's Conditionality Principle''':
: If <math>\ E\ </math> is any experiment having the form of a mixture of component experiments <math>\ E_h\ ,</math> then for each outcome <math>\ \bigl(\ E_h, x_h\ \bigr)\ </math> of <math>\ E\ ,</math> the evidential meaning of any outcome <math>\ x\ </math> of any mixture experiment <math>\ E\ </math> is the same as that of the corresponding outcome <math>\ x_h\ </math> of the corresponding component experiment <math>\ E_h\ </math> actually conducted, ignoring the overall structure of the mixed experiment; ''see'' {{harvp|Birnbaum|1962}}.

=== Examples ===
An illustration of the conditionality principle, in a [[bioinformatics]] context, is given by {{harvp|Barker|2014}}.

;Example scenario:
The ancillary statistic <math>\ h\ </math> could be the roll of [[dice|die]], whose value will be one of  <math>\ h = 1, \ldots\ ,\ 6 ~.</math> This random selection of an experiment is actually a wise precaution to curb the influence of a researchers' biases, if there is reason to suspect that the researcher might consciously or unconsciously select an experiment that seems like it would be likely to produce data that supports a favored hypothesis. The result of the dice roll then determines which of six possible experiments <math>\ E_1, \ldots\ ,\ E_6\ ,</math> is the one actually conducted to obtain the study's data.

Say that the die rolls a '3'. In that case, the result observed for <math>\ x\ </math> is actually <math>\ x_3\ ,</math> the outcome of experminent <math>\ E_3 ~.</math> None of the other five experiments <math>\ E_1, E_2, E_4, E_5, ~~ \mathsf{ or } ~~ E_6\ </math> is ever conducted, and none of the other possible results is ever seen, <math>\ x_1, x_2, x_4, x_5, ~~ \mathsf{or} ~~ x_6\ ,</math> that ''might'' have been observed if some other number than '3' had come up. The actual observed outcome, <math>\ x_3\ ,</math> is unaffected by any aspect of the other five sub-experiments that were ''not'' carried out, and only the procedures and [[experimental design]] of <math>\ E_3\ ,</math> the sub-experiment that ''was'' conducted to collect the data, <math>\ x_3\ ,</math> had any bearing on the statistical analysis the outcome, regardless of the fact that the [[experimental design]]s for the experiments which ''might'' have been conducted had been prepared at the time of the actual experiment <math>\ E_3\ ,</math> and might just as likely been performed.

The conditionality principle says that all of the details of  <math>\ E_1, E_2, E_4, E_5, ~~ \mathsf{ or } ~~ E_6\ </math> ''must'' be excluded from the statistical analysis of the ''actual'' observation <math>\ x_3\ ,</math> and even the fact that experiment 3 was chosen by the roll of a die: Further, none of the possible randomness brought into the outcome by the statistic <math>\ h\ </math> (the dice roll) can be included in the analysis either. The only thing that determines the correct statistics to be used for the data analysis is experiment <math>\ E_3\ ,</math> and the only data to consider is <math>\ x_3\ ,</math> not <math>\ h = 3 ~.</math>
